newsitem.title: USA: CBOT's new trading floor passes the Greenspan test.
newsitem.headline: CBOT's new trading floor passes the Greenspan test.

text.p: The first real test of the Chicago Board of Trade's new financial trading floor almost didn't happen because of software glitch Wednesday morning.

Early in the session, trade was halted for 40 minutes on the week-old 60,000 square foot, $182 million financial futures facility because of a technical problem with the CBOT's price reporting system software.
An already nervous market waited anxiously for trade to resume with less than an hour to go before the start of key testimony by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan.
Trade reopened quietly at 0810 CST/1410 GMT, only to be jerked to attention by the first part of Greenspan's semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins remarks at 0900 CST.
As the Fed chief warned of the potential for a tighter credit policy, Treasury bond futures collapsed, putting the CBOT's new floor to the test in fast market trading.

"It was chaos," said Brad Tyl, a vice president of Aubrey G. Lanston who is stationed on the floor. "The first trade was (in the) 112-00 handle and then we had a straight shot down to the 111-7/32 low," he said of March Treasury bonds. March eventually posted a low at 110-25/32.
Each move of 1/32 point in the bond contract is worth $31.25, meaning an owner of one contract lost at least $781.25 on the first move after Greenspan's testimony.
"It was about as rough as we've had it in a couple of years," Tyl said.
The day's volume in T-bond futures was the largest in nearly three years. According to exchange volume estimates, 735,00 contracts traded on Wednesday, the highest since 737,065 on May 6, 1994.
If preliminary estimates are accurate, it would be the third highest volume in Treasury bond futures ever, despite the 40-minute trading halt.
Many traders said the new trading facility held up well in its first trial by fire.
One bond options trader said players had been waiting for the first heavy volume day to "show the cracks" in the new trading floor. He said it passed the test well.
Tyl agreed. "This is the first one, and we had a couple little blisters here and there, but by and large we made it through just fine," he said. "I think customers understood."
